defects: Only 3 shots in 15 s and the longest runs 5.9 s. The marquee section is several seconds of rows scrolling at constant speed with no shift in the choreography.
The scrolling rows of OFFSET move linearly, with no easing in or out and no difference in speed between rows that would give parallax or weight.
The CMYK split-plate 'Offset' frame drifts by small amounts between samples. The plates do not snap into register or overshoot, so the core 'offset' gesture never pays off with a satisfying lock.
The opening frame is a cropped blue 'O' against a mostly empty cream field. It reads as an unfinished push-in, not a composed image.
The final lockup goes static for about 2.5 s (per-second change of 6.1, 2.6, 9.8). The registration shift on the logo is barely visible, so the hold feels dead rather than resolved.
There is a stray speck or pixel artifact above the logo in the final-section pair (right frame, upper centre).
Small metadata type in the end card (Design Systems Conference / Lisboa / dates) is very small and low-weight at 1080p, and on the edge of being legible at broadcast viewing size.
The section-to-section energy curve peaks early (high change from about 5 to 9 s, 33-60%), then drops sharply instead of building to a late peak.
gaps: Motion: the misregistration idea is strong but is played as a static overlay and a linear marquee. Top studio work would choreograph the plates: separate, slip and snap into register with overshoot and settle, stagger the rows with different speeds and eases, and use match-cut transitions built from the plate shift itself instead of 3 hard sections.

Pace and arc: shots run too long for the format, energy peaks in the middle and then dies, and the end lockup goes static too early. It needs more in-shot development, a peak at 70% where all plates collide, and a short, earned settle into register.

Sound: the riser into the 6 s drop and the clicks timed to cuts are competent, but the bed is a dense, static synth wall with little dynamic shaping. It needs printing-press texture (rollers, paper, registration clicks) tied to the plate moves, and real headroom and contrast before the payoff.
